title: Build a bursary application that is ready to submit
summary: A practical document checklist, funding comparison and submission routine for South African learners.

sections.title: Start with eligibility, then build a shortlist
sections.body: Before writing a motivational letter, read the provider’s criteria and separate compulsory requirements from preferences. Record the qualification, institution, study year, academic requirements and any location or household circumstances mentioned. If a rule is unclear, ask the provider using contact details on its official website. An attractive award is not useful if your programme is excluded. Make a shortlist of opportunities that fit your situation and keep a separate record for options that need clarification. This prevents you from spending all your available time on an application you cannot qualify for.

sections.title: Prepare a document folder without oversharing
sections.body: Use the application instructions as your checklist rather than a generic social media list. A provider may request identification, recent results, proof of admission and financial supporting documents, but requirements differ. Check that scans are readable, complete and within the portal’s file limits. Use clear filenames such as Surname_Results.pdf and store originals securely. Upload sensitive documents only through a verified application channel. Never publish identity numbers, bank details or full household documents in a community post. If certified copies are requested, check the provider’s rules about certification and recency before submitting.

sections.title: Compare the full funding offer
sections.body: Two bursaries with similar headlines may cover very different costs. Write down whether tuition, registration, books, accommodation, transport and meals are covered, capped or excluded. Read the renewal conditions and any service, work or repayment obligations in the agreement. Ask how payments are made and what happens if you change course or repeat a module. For a personal budget, subtract confirmed support from your expected costs and label any outstanding funding as uncertain. A submitted application is not an award, so keep a realistic backup plan while waiting for a decision.

sections.title: Submit, save evidence and follow up
sections.body: Check that your name and identification details match across the form and supporting documents. Answer each written question with a specific example from your own experience. Explain your study goal, preparation and circumstances honestly; do not copy another applicant’s story. Submit before the final day where possible, save the confirmation or reference number, and note when the provider says it will respond. Check your inbox and spam folder for requests. If you need to follow up, include the reference and a short question. Keep a tracker with the official link, deadline, submission date, outstanding documents and final outcome.

sources.title: NSFAS official website — check its own requirements

title: Prepare for NSFAS without falling for application scams
summary: Keep control of your account, follow official instructions and distinguish an application from confirmed funding.

sections.title: Use the official starting point
sections.body: Start at the NSFAS website and follow its links to the application channel. A message with a logo or a familiar-looking profile is not proof that it comes from NSFAS. The official guidance states that applying is free and warns applicants against sharing passwords or one-time passwords. Do not pay a stranger who promises approval or a faster result. If someone is helping you use a computer, enter your own credentials and sign out afterwards. Type the website address yourself when a forwarded link looks suspicious.

sections.title: Prepare your information before opening the form
sections.body: Read the current instructions for your application cycle and situation. Use the names and identification details shown on your official records and keep access to your own phone number and email. Check the documents the official system actually requests; do not assume a checklist from a previous year applies unchanged. Prepare readable files and keep a private backup. When household information is requested, answer accurately and ask the official support channel if a category does not fit your circumstances. Do not guess an answer just to move to the next screen.

sections.title: Admission and funding require separate attention
sections.body: Being admitted to a programme does not by itself mean your study costs have been funded. Likewise, submitting a funding application does not confirm a final award. Check both your institution’s admission process and the NSFAS funding process. The official NSFAS information explains that funding depends on the relevant eligibility rules and approved qualifications at eligible public universities or TVET colleges. Before committing to costs, verify your own programme and status through the appropriate official channels. Treat online estimates and community advice as starting points rather than individual funding decisions.

sections.title: Track the application and respond carefully
sections.body: Save your application reference and check the official account for status changes or document requests. Read the exact wording of any notice rather than relying on a screenshot shared by another applicant. If a decision offers a review or appeal route, follow the instructions and deadline attached to your decision. Keep copies of submissions and confirmations. When asking for help in a public group, remove identification numbers, addresses and reference numbers from screenshots. For current dates, eligibility rules, allowances and support contacts, return to the NSFAS website; these details can change between cycles.

title: Compare a university or TVET course before you apply
summary: Look beyond the course title: compare requirements, recognition, practical training and the full cost.

sections.title: Work backwards from the work you want to do
sections.body: Write down the kind of work that interests you and the tasks you would expect to perform. Then compare the actual modules, practical components and progression routes in each programme. Similar course titles can describe different qualifications. Ask what graduates can progress to, whether workplace experience is included and how that experience is arranged. If the career has a professional registration requirement, verify that route with the relevant professional body. A promotional claim should be checked against the institution’s official programme information before you pay an application or registration fee.

sections.title: Check recognition and the exact programme
sections.body: Verify the institution and the qualification rather than relying on a certificate image or a promise in an advertisement. The Department of Higher Education and Training publishes registers for checking private institutions. Match the legal institution name, campus and programme details carefully and ask questions where the information does not agree. Registration and accreditation checks can involve different bodies depending on the qualification. If you cannot establish who awards the qualification and which recognition applies, pause payment and request written clarification. Keep the documents you used to make your decision.

sections.title: Build a comparison table with real costs
sections.body: For each option, record duration, subject prerequisites, minimum marks, application process, campus and travel requirements. Add tuition, registration, equipment, data, accommodation and transport to your budget. Distinguish an advertised fee from the total annual cost and ask about refund rules before paying a deposit. Compare learning support, disability support, access to laboratories or workshops and realistic travel time. A course that looks cheaper on tuition alone may be harder to complete if daily transport costs or timetable clashes are high. Mark any unknown costs so you can follow them up.

sections.title: Keep more than one realistic route open
sections.body: Choose a small set of programmes that fit your academic profile and interests, including an alternative route you would be willing to take. Read each institution’s current prospectus rather than assuming all applications use the same points system or dates. Keep your application reference and check whether an offer is conditional, provisional or final. Respond through the official channel and verify acceptance deadlines. Before registration, confirm that the campus, qualification and fee arrangement match the offer you accepted. Never treat an application confirmation as a place secured or a funding guarantee.

title: Understand admission points and subject requirements
summary: Calculate carefully, check each institution’s rules and plan alternatives without treating an estimate as an offer.

sections.title: There is no single points rule for every course
sections.body: Admission point scores help institutions interpret school results, but the calculation and exclusions can differ. A university may publish a general points table and then set additional rules for particular programmes. Another programme may consider individual subjects, selection tests or other evidence. Begin with the exact qualification and the current prospectus for the year you intend to enter. Record which subjects are included, how percentages convert to points and whether any subjects are treated differently. Do not apply a points table from one institution to another without checking it.

sections.title: Separate overall points from subject minimums
sections.body: A total above the stated threshold may still be insufficient if you do not meet a required subject mark. Create one line for each compulsory subject and compare your result with the published requirement. Pay particular attention when a programme distinguishes Mathematics from Mathematical Literacy or specifies a language or science subject. Meeting minimum requirements can still leave selection conditions outstanding. If your results are pending, note whether the institution considers the results you currently have and what final conditions apply. Ask admissions directly when the wording is unclear.

sections.title: Use a worked planning example correctly
sections.body: Imagine an institution’s own table gives your selected subjects points of 6, 5, 5, 4, 4 and 3. Their sum is 27. This is only an example of adding points after the applicable conversion rules have been established; it is not a national conversion table. Next check each programme-specific subject rule. A required subject below its minimum can matter even when the total is high enough. Finally record any further selection requirement. Keep the prospectus page or link beside your calculation so you can explain where every rule came from.

sections.title: Use the result to choose your next action
sections.body: Compare your estimate with several programmes that interest you. If you meet the listed minimums, complete the official application and continue tracking the institution’s response. If you fall short, ask about recognised alternative routes and the conditions attached to them. An extended programme, different qualification or later application may have its own entry rules; do not assume transfer is automatic. Recalculate when your final results arrive. An online calculator can support planning, but only the institution can decide admission and communicate an offer through its official process.

title: Turn past papers into a study plan that targets weak topics
summary: A repeatable routine for timed practice, useful marking and checking whether your understanding has improved.

sections.title: Choose a paper that matches your course
sections.body: Start with your subject, grade, language and the relevant curriculum or assessment guidance. Check whether a paper uses an older format before treating its mark allocation as a guide to your next exam. The Department of Basic Education provides an official past-paper resource for National Senior Certificate revision. Use the matching memorandum and any required answer book or source material. Download the files while you have a reliable connection, name them clearly and keep the paper separate from the memorandum until you have attempted the questions.

sections.title: Attempt first, then mark honestly
sections.body: Choose a quiet practice period and write under a realistic time limit. Read instructions about question choice, calculators, diagrams and working. Record where you became stuck without opening the memorandum immediately. When marking, distinguish a correct method with a calculation error from a wrong method or a missing concept. Do not award yourself full credit because an answer looks familiar. Use the memorandum to understand the expected reasoning and ask a teacher about equivalent methods or marking decisions you cannot resolve. Keep the original attempt so you can compare it with later work.

sections.title: Make an error log that changes your revision
sections.body: For each significant error, record the question, topic, reason for losing marks and a specific next action. “Study harder” is too vague. A useful action might be to practise drawing force diagrams, explain a biological process without notes, or compare two sources before writing a history paragraph. Group repeated mistakes so you can see whether the main problem is knowledge, interpretation, method or time management. Work through the underlying concept in a textbook or with a teacher before attempting another set. Rewriting the memorandum alone may hide a gap in understanding.

sections.title: Retest with unfamiliar questions
sections.body: After targeted revision, attempt a different question on the same concept without looking at your corrected answer. Explain the reasoning in words as well as calculations where appropriate. If the mistake returns, adjust the next study session rather than repeating full papers without feedback. As the exam approaches, mix topics and practise deciding which method to use. Track accuracy and completion time separately. A steady improvement across unfamiliar questions is more useful evidence of progress than a high score on a paper whose answers you have already memorised.

title: Make a school-leaver plan with dates, costs and alternatives
summary: Bring study choices, applications, document preparation and a realistic student budget into one tracker.

sections.title: Use one tracker for separate processes
sections.body: Create a table with a row for every institution, programme and funding application. Include the official link, required documents, closing date, reference number and next action. Keep admission, accommodation and funding as separate entries when they have different processes. A successful step in one does not automatically complete the others. Check dates on official pages and record when you checked them. Put reminders before deadlines so there is time to resolve a missing document or an account access problem. Do not wait until your final results to start researching routes that accept earlier applications.

sections.title: Budget for the months before the first class
sections.body: List the costs that may arise before teaching starts as well as the annual study expenses. These can include application charges where applicable, document preparation, travel, registration, equipment and an accommodation deposit. For each cost, record the amount, due date and whether support is confirmed. Do not count an unapproved bursary as money already available. Ask the institution or accommodation provider about payment and refund terms before committing. A simple cash-flow calendar helps you notice a payment gap early enough to investigate options through official support channels.

sections.title: Choose an alternative you would actually use
sections.body: Discuss at least one alternative route with a teacher, careers adviser or admissions office. Compare its entry requirements, qualification outcome, total cost and possible progression. Avoid choosing an option only because it sounds like an easy transfer into a different programme; progression needs to be verified. If you consider work or a gap period, identify a specific goal such as improving a subject result, gaining relevant experience or saving toward a known cost. Give that goal a timetable and a review date so the plan has practical next steps.

sections.title: Review offers and protect your information
sections.body: Before accepting, check the qualification, campus, conditions, response deadline and payment instructions against the institution’s official channels. Be cautious when a social media message promises a guaranteed place or asks you to send sensitive documents to a personal account. Keep your passwords and one-time passwords private. Tell a trusted person where you store application records without giving them unnecessary access to your accounts. Review your tracker weekly during busy application periods and update it when results or decisions arrive. A useful plan changes as reliable information becomes available.
